Flashboys or Superforecasters?

A deep dive into Polymarket’s user-base growth and portraits

Key findings

Based on 787 million deduplicated fills across 1,733,011 wallets on Polymarket’s international exchange, Jan–Jun 2026, plus venue-level data for Polymarket US.

  • A second Polymarket emerged. The CFTC-regulated US venue grew from 5% of the international book’s monthly volume in January to 47% by June — on separate rails, with deliberately opaque user data.
  • The user base is three tribes. Retail is 89% of wallets but 23% of volume; ~102K probable bots take two-thirds of all volume and make 89% of fills; a small informed/pro cohort trades big tickets in few markets, mostly by resting orders.
  • Acquisition is a portfolio, not a hit. New users enter through dozens of timely listings — the biggest single onboarding market of any month captures ~3% of that month’s new wallets — then cross-sell toward sports, crypto and geopolitics.
  • Category loyalty is weak; platform loyalty is real. ~51–57% of actives return the next month, but far fewer stay in the category that brought them in.
  • Trading is a transfer. Gross PnL nets to zero: retail (−$74M) and pros (−$26M) fund the bot cohort (+$108M) — yet the median bot wallet loses, and only 146 of 1.75M wallets were profitable all six months.
I
Part I
Growth overview of the two Polymarket venues

The rise of Polymarket US

Polymarket spent H1 2026 becoming two exchanges — and the discourse only watched one of them. The original venue — global for non-US customers, an off-chain CLOB with on-chain settlement on Polygon — Polymarket International cleared $17.9B of one-sided volume in six months and held stable through the summer, even as commentators read the headline chart as a loss of ground to Kalshi. The quiet part of the story is its younger sibling: the CFTC-regulated Polymarket US, launched in late 2025, went from a rounding error to nearly half the international book’s monthly volume by June — and two-thirds of it by July.

The two share a brand but not order books, not a user base, and — as we will see — a very different composition of market catalog and revenue engine. What they do share, with each other and with Kalshi, is market design at a high level: all three venues run central limit order books with off-chain matching, charging takers on the same price-sensitive curve — fee = Θ·C·p(1−p). The international venue settles every fill on Polygon in public; Polymarket US clears the identical mechanics on a private CFTC-regulated ledger. Same engine, different rails.

A note on conventions before any cross-venue number: every venue’s headline volume follows its own definition. Throughout this report, volume refers to single-leg, taker-side dollars — a stricter measure that runs below the headline figures. Kalshi reports contracts at $1 face value regardless of traded price (the notional-volume convention); Polymarket’s public feed logs every fill twice; similarly, the Polymarket US dataset’s default column is both-sides contract value. Put July on one measuring stick — one-sided dollars actually traded, counted once — and the conventional $41B / $7B / $5B become $13.3B / $3.0B / $2.0B.

Where open interest parks, where volume and fees print

Volume and open interest measure different aspects of the business, and the daily turnover ratio — dollars traded over collateral locked, the same stick for every venue — reveals how differently the market categories behave. Sports and crypto are the fastest-turning markets, generating the most volume and fees from a given open-interest base; World/Geopolitics is the slowest as of July, turning over just 0.01–0.02× a day on both Polymarket and Kalshi. And because the same category converges to the same speed across platforms — sports clears roughly 0.6× a day on all three venues — turnover is an attribute of the market category, not the venue. The outlier is Kalshi’s crypto book, which turns its open interest over nearly six times a day — $96M of daily flow against $17M of capital, with 98% of that volume in markets that live three hours or less. Politics is the opposite extreme: on both venues it is where capital parks, a quarter-billion dollars of open interest each against single-digit millions a day of trading.

The comparison also reframes the venue race. Kalshi’s headline open-interest lead over Polymarket comes entirely from its sports book, and its blended turnover (0.44× a day) is dragged below Polymarket US’s (0.64×) by that $290M political shelf — the largest parked-capital pile in the industry. The US venue, 88% near-term sports by open interest with no shelf at all, is pound-for-pound the fastest book of the three.

It helps to see what parked capital actually is — and is not. A first-principles audit of the mint-and-burn flows shows the average 5-minute up-or-down market only ever locks about $2,800 of collateral: the markets that do 90% of the category’s volume hold essentially none of its capital, turning over dozens of times a day. The open interest lives elsewhere — in a shelf of dated threshold markets (a ladder of “will Bitcoin dip to $35–55K by December 31” insurance strikes, year-end lottery tickets like “Bitcoin $100K,” and, the single largest holder at $1.4M, “Will Satoshi move any Bitcoin in 2026”) plus a tail of already-resolved collateral still awaiting redemption, which this open-interest convention is known to include. Kalshi’s is not: it auto-settles cash at expiry, so its open interest carries no dead tail — one more convention asymmetry to keep in mind when comparing ratios. Buy once, wait for December. A category’s turnover ratio is really just the share of its open interest that lives in markets that still trade.

The broader lesson of this section: cross-venue turnover and volume comparisons measure catalogs, not integrity. Volume can be flattered by convention or manufactured by product mix; the one number strangers must actually put up and leave on the table is open interest — which is why this report leans on it wherever the venues are compared.

The turnover riddles, resolved

Short-dated crypto is the highest-velocity product in prediction markets — 15-minute up/down books recycle their capital several times a day by construction. Right now only Kalshi has onboarded it at critical mass: $96M/day of taker flow vs Polymarket’s $15M. That one product line is most of the gap between the venues’ headline turnover.

Sports is the second-fastest — and the one product every venue carries in size. It is also the engine of Polymarket US’s rise: 88% of the US venue’s open interest is sports, and a book made entirely of this week’s games is exactly why the youngest venue turns its capital fastest (0.64× a day).

The transferable lesson: measured on one stick, the same product behaves the same everywhere. Sports clears ~0.6× a day on all three venues — Kalshi 0.57, Polymarket 0.67, Polymarket US 0.64 — despite fee coefficients ranging from 0.03 to 0.07 on the same curve. Retail takers are fee-insensitive; gamblers just pay the vig. Turnover is product physics, not venue magic.

But retail is only half the tape — and that makes the ratio a diagnostic. Professional flow is the opposite of fee-insensitive: its existence depends entirely on fee terms, and subsidies are not a point on the same dial — they flip the sign of trading costs for specific accounts. So when a category’s turnover diverges hard from its cross-venue peers, one of two things is true: the catalog inside the label differs (Polymarket “crypto” is a long-dated insurance shelf; Kalshi “crypto” is a 15-minute casino — same label, opposite products), or the professional flow is being priced differently (subsidized market makers, volume rebates, discounted fee tiers — all of which exist in CFTC rule filings). The same product shows both halves at once: Polymarket’s crypto micro-market bot flow bled out after its fee rollout, while Kalshi’s LP-subsidized 15-minute books boomed. Retail doesn’t respond to fees; bots respond to nothing else.

Inside Polymarket US

The US venue’s entire life fits in four daily series. Volume compounds from ~$1M a day at launch to $50–100M a day by July; transactions cross a million a day; open interest peaks above $150M. Fees switch on in January at a flat basis point, then move in April to the price-sensitive formula both venues now share.

The fee engine is real, and bigger than the community datasets suggest: $30M of gross taker fees in June alone. Working through the official rebate schedule — a 25% maker rebate at the point of trade, a promotional all-taker rebate that expired April 30, then volume-tiered taker rebates — puts modeled retained revenue near $17M for June, roughly double the flat-25% assumption most trackers carry. Where the anonymized tape can’t identify who qualifies for tiers, the share of fees from large takers is modeled on the international venue’s mix, where the top 0.3% of takers do ~63% of the volume.

Why the user analysis covers the international venue

Polymarket US (QCX LLC, a CFTC-designated contract market) clears on an internal ledger through FCM intermediaries. It leaves no on-chain footprint, its public trade stream is anonymized to side-and-intent by design, and no leaderboard or profile surfaces exist. The international venue is the opposite: every fill carries a wallet address, publicly. One platform, radically different transparency — so every per-user analysis in this report is built on the international venue’s on-chain order flow. First-party US user statistics would require a data partnership with the venue.

What the world bets on

What is the world betting on? Half of everything traded is sports. Crypto follows at roughly 30% — overwhelmingly five-minute up-or-down micro-markets, though its single largest market is the controversial “MicroStrategy sells any Bitcoin by May 31” ($95M). World/Geopolitics ranks third at ~15%. What varies more than volume is concentration: Sports’ biggest market is a rounding error within its category (0.27%), while a single “will the US confirm aliens exist” market is a quarter of Science & Tech.

What the international venue earns

The international venue generated roughly $184M in H1 gross fees — gross, not net revenue, since maker rebates and incentives come out of that. Category economics differ sharply: with only half the volume, Crypto printed more fees than Sports, and together the two account for 98% of it. World/Geopolitics, third by volume, runs deliberately fee-free.

II
Part II
Polymarket International: user cohorts by market catalog

1.7 million wallets, two roles

Everything user-level starts from one number: 1,733,011 wallets traded on the international venue in H1. But the two sides of the order book are not symmetric populations — nearly every wallet has taken liquidity at least once, while fewer than half have ever rested a limit order. The maker side is the professional side, and it is small.

How the numbers were cleaned: three findings from the raw data

Three properties of the raw on-chain data shape every number in this report.

Volume is double-counted at the source. For every taker order, the exchange logs the per-maker fills and one aggregate record with the exchange contract in the taker field. Summing everything inflates volume roughly 2× — the convention behind Polymarket’s self-reported figures. We drop the aggregate rows: H1 one-sided volume is $17.9B, not ~$36.8B.

Splits and merges are halves, not duplicates. Minting a YES/NO pair logs two rows that sum to the collateral moved — they are summed as-is.

Redemption rows are duplicated (proven by conservation: a wallet that only ever bought 40 shares shows 80 “redeemed”), and an infrastructure address batch-redeems on users’ behalf — both are corrected in the profit-and-loss accounting.

Concentration, from both sides of the book

Prediction markets are often described as democratic; the volume says otherwise, and it says so more sharply for supply than demand. The top thousand makers provide the majority of all resting liquidity. On the demand side, six percent of wallets — the hyperactive tier — do four-fifths of the taking, while a third of all wallets place five or fewer trades in six months.

Two rails, one order book

Structurally, flow splits between standalone binary markets and mutually-exclusive multi-outcome sets (elections, “who will win X”). Binaries carry three-quarters of the volume; multi-outcome markets punch above their volume in reach, touching a disproportionate share of users.

Growth accounting: where each month’s users come from

User growth tells a less flattering story than volume: monthly active wallets were nearly flat across the half — 580K in January to 594K in June — despite 1.1M wallets trading for the first time. Each month, 43–49% of the prior month’s active wallets stopped trading, with churn peaking at 358K in April, forcing the platform to continually refill the funnel with new and resurrected wallets. Acquisition was strong — peaking in March — but active-wallet retention is the bottleneck.

Three caveats before reading too much into that. A wallet is not always a user. Some “churn” is users rotating into fresh wallets. And churn here means a wallet stopped trading — not that an account was closed or unfunded, the way a fintech like Robinhood would define it in a filing.

Where new users come from

Attribute each new wallet to the first market it ever touched and the acquisition machine becomes visible. Three categories do almost all the onboarding, each with its own season: crypto peaking at 99K new wallets in March, geopolitics at 68K in January, sports at 91K in June — the World Cup’s opening month. And no single market did it all: major events bring waves (January’s Iran headlines, June’s Taiwan market and the World Cup), yet even the top onboarding market brought in fewer than 7K of H1’s 1.13M new wallets. Categories win in aggregate; acquisition is a portfolio, not a hit.

Do they stay?

About half of any month’s active wallets trade again the following month — but loyalty to a category is far weaker than loyalty to the platform. Users churn out of the market type that brought them in and reappear somewhere else.

Do entry markets shape retention? Mostly not. Retention clusters tightly across nearly all categories — 44–49% of new wallets remain active after one month, 25–32% after three — regardless of the door they came through. The one clear outlier is Crypto, whose entrants retain roughly 30% lower than every other category’s.

The user matrix

The cross-sell engine in one picture: for every pair of categories, the share of the smaller category’s users who also trade the other. The headline surprise is at the top: Sports × Crypto overlap is only 49% — despite being the two largest user groups, they are two large but meaningfully distinct retail audiences, with Sports users expanding into other categories more readily than Crypto users, who tend to stay inside Crypto.

World/Geopolitics is the strongest connective layer, with consistently high overlap against everything — evidence that news markets are a core product for the international venue, attracting the audience with the broadest interest across the platform.

The coordinates of loyalty and expansion

Put onboarding, retention and cross-sell on one plane and every acquisition channel gets coordinates: loyalty — whether a category’s new users are still on the platform a month later — against expansion — how many other categories its users end up trading. Six of seven categories cluster at 43–49% loyalty, arranged along a spectrum from Sports’ loyal homebodies to Science & Tech’s engaged explorers, whose users average 3.6 other categories.

Crypto sits alone in the bottom-left: 37% loyalty and the least expansion. The five-minute casino acquires tourists — users who neither stay nor branch out. For a venue deciding what to list next, this is the acquisition-quality menu: sports buys retention, niche categories buy cross-sell, crypto buys volume that leaves.

III
Part III
Market microstructure: user profiles, timing and profitability

Breadth, habit, and the shape of engagement

Before any behavioral labels, two plain facts. First, breadth correlates with size: wallets that touch all seven categories are one percent of the population and trade seven times the volume per wallet of pure specialists. Second, most wallet-market relationships are one or two fills — except in news markets, where users return to the same question again and again as headlines move.

The three tribes

Classify every wallet by how it behaves — frequency, sizing uniformity, breadth, ticket size — and the user base resolves into three tribes. Retail is nine wallets in ten. Probable bots are one in seventeen, and they take two-thirds of all volume and account for nine of every ten fills. The informed/pro cohort is the smallest and quietest: big tickets, few markets, and a preference for resting orders over taking.

By category, the same picture repeats with different intensity: bots own the two biggest categories outright, while the contested middle — geopolitics, finance, culture — is where humans still set the price.

Ticket sizes

The tribes are visible in the distribution of individual fills: retail and bots cluster in single-digit-dollar tickets, while the pro cohort’s distribution sits two orders of magnitude to the right.

Are users fee-sensitive?

Fees arrived at different times in different categories — a natural experiment, with fee-free World/Geopolitics as the control. The composition of volume shifts visibly around each category’s fee date; the composition of wallets barely moves. Fees changed how much each tribe trades far more than who shows up.

The fee rollout, as a reference

Crypto — coefficient 0.07: Jan 5 (15-minute pilot) → Feb 12 (5-minute) → Mar 6 (all new crypto markets)

Sports — 0.03, from Feb 18

Weather & Culture — 0.05; Finance & Sci-Tech — 0.04: from Mar 30 (“fee structure v2”)

World / Geopolitics — fee-free throughout (the control group)

Maker rebates from Apr 17: 20% of gross (crypto), 25% (others). Fees follow fee = Θ·C·p(1−p) — highest at 50¢, vanishing at the extremes.

Entry timing by cohorts

Within a market’s life, when do the tribes act? Sports and crypto are the most latency-competitive: every cohort’s median entry lands in the final tenth of the market’s window — adversarial selection pressure for anyone slow. Weather is the opposite extreme: entries come early, consistent with outcomes that models can price long before resolution — and it is the one category where pros wait longest relative to retail.

User PnL: who actually makes money?

Add up every dollar that flowed through every wallet’s positions in markets resolved during H1 and the ledger closes at zero — before fees, trading is a transfer, not a factory. A third of wallets ended positive; the tails balance almost perfectly.

Split the ledger by tribe and the transfer has a direction: retail and pros fund the bot cohort’s gains. But the sharpest finding cuts the other way — the median bot wallet loses money. The class’s profit is carried by a small number of large operations, and persistence is vanishingly rare: of 1.75 million wallets, 146 were profitable in all six months.

How PnL is measured

Realized PnL per wallet and market, for markets resolved within H1: signed cash flows (buys and splits out; sells, merges and redemptions in) plus terminal settlement of residual shares at resolution — each market a closed loop, no cost-basis accounting needed. Figures are gross of fees; the tiers netting to ~$0 across two million wallets is the accounting identity closing, and subtracting the ~$184M of H1 fees pushes the aggregate negative. The approach follows Sergeenkov’s cash-flow method with the terminal-settlement refinement of Dai, Jia & Yu (arXiv:2606.31675). Addresses are not people: multi-wallet operations are invisible to any per-address accounting.

Synthesis

Listings are the product

[Placeholder — to be reworked after the full-draft read-through.] The evidence assembled here supports the acquisition thesis this report set out to test: onboarding is dispersed across dozens of timely listings, category loyalty is weak while platform retention is strong, and the cross-sell matrix funnels every niche audience toward the same fat-tail destinations. Listings acquire; sports, crypto and geopolitics retain; bots supply the liquidity that makes small markets tradable — and collect the transfer for doing so.

Methodology

Methodology & data notes

Scope. All per-user analysis covers Polymarket’s international exchange (Polygon CTF/NegRisk contracts), Jan 1 – Jun 30, 2026, deduplicated to one record per fill and filtered of post-resolution dust (price 0.5¢–99.5¢). Polymarket US appears at venue level only. A wallet is “active” in a month if it participated in at least one fill.

Conventions. Volume is one-sided notional attributed to the taker ($17.877B H1) — roughly half the double-counted convention in public reporting. Users are unions of maker and taker addresses; exchange contracts are excluded. Categories follow a consolidated seven-category taxonomy validated market-by-market. The behavioral classification is frozen once and reused in every cohort chart.

Fees are reconstructed from the official schedule (shares × rate × p(1−p)) because the indexed fee field is unreliable after the April V2 exchange migration.

Sources. On-chain data indexed by Surf; Polymarket US daily aggregates from the community Dune dataset by @datadashboards (venue revenue after April reflects the uploader’s flat-25% assumption and is a lower bound). Every query behind this report is published alongside it.

The data in this report is assembled by Surf AI. To integrate the same data into your own products or research, contact James Dai.
